The Executive Director City Futures submitted a
report containing the Annual Report in respect of the
Council’s International Activity during the 2025-26 Municipal
Year. On 15 October 2025 the Strategy & Resources Policy
Committee approved the Sheffield International Strategy 2025-28 and
this report outlines some of the main activities that have taken
place towards delivering key themes within the International
Strategy.
 
2025 marked the 75th Anniversary of Sheffield
Twinning with the German city of Bochum – the report outlines
activities that took place during 2025 to mark this significant
milestone. The Appendix attached to this Report provides a detailed
overview of international engagement. 




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That Strategy and
Resources Policy Committee:-




 


 




 


(a) note the
contents of the International Update 2025-26 included at Appendix A
attached to the report;
 
(b) notes the
activities that have taken place during 2025 to mark the 75th
Anniversary of Sheffield Twinning with the German city of Bochum;
and
 
(c) notes the
progress made towards delivering some of the key themes contained
within the International Strategy 2025-28.




 


 




12.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




12.3.1


The Report
presents the Council’s third annual International Update, and
provides a transparent overview of Sheffield’s activities
within the international arena during 2025-26.




 


 




12.3.2


It is 4 months since the International Strategy 2025-28 was
approved.  During 2025 a lot has been
achieved, despite the Strategy, itself, having only been approved
for a relatively short period of time.




 


 




12.3.3


Bochum is Sheffield’s oldest Twin City, the relationship
having been established in 1950.  It is
pleasing to note that 75 years on, the relationship between both
cities is very much alive and it is fitting that so many things
have taken place to acknowledge the anniversary during
2025.  In addition, it is fantastic to
witness the efforts of our universities to engage with each other
in meaningful ways to cement this relationship between our two
cities even further.




 


 




12.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


Alternative Option: ‘Do Nothing’ - The alternative
option would be not to engage internationally.  Given the International Strategy 2025-28 was only
approved by Strategy and Resources Policy Committee on 15 October
2025 acknowledging the need to formalise our international
activities, inactivity would not be
appropriate.

content:
11.1


The Executive Director City Futures submitted a
report summaring options for
introducing free travel for children and young people in Sheffield,
including indicative cost drivers, justification and evidence base,
key assumptions, risks and financial sustainability
considerations.
 
The report sets out options for a potential
January–July 2027 pilot and recommends further development
work subject to Committee direction, to include funding parameters,
detailed network analysis and agreement with operators. The report
confirmed that it is an options and scoping report. It does not
commit the Council to implement a scheme or to allocate funding at
this stage.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That Strategy and
Resources Policy Committee:-




 


 




 


(a) notes that
the earliest a free travel pilot could commence in Sheffield would
be January 2027 and this will require concerted work from March
2026, with a decision around whether Members wish to proceed sought
at the first Strategy and Resources committee meeting following the
May 2026 local elections. It is recommended that officers prepare
further information to support this decision at that meeting;
 
(b) notes that
costs of a pilot will need to be funded by Sheffield City Council
(SCC) for any period up until South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined
Authority (SYMCA) launch free bus travel (anticipated to be late
Summer 2027);
 
(c) notes that
there is widespread political support for the provision of free bus
travel for children and young people across the council;
and
 
(d) notes as
context for this report that SYMCA is not planning to introduce
free travel for under 22s (U22) in the region. The Mayor's transport vision, launched on 16th March
2026, indicates that the focus for the Mayor is provision for under 18s (U18). Therefore, a
free travel proposal for U22 in Sheffield would result in ongoing
annual costs to SCC, exposing the council to a significant and
unquantifiable financial liability. As such, it is recommended that
officers work with SYMCA to explore a pilot limited to U18 free
travel only, noting that there is currently no identified budget
for such a pilot.




 


 




11.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




11.3.1


The options set
out enable the Committee to provide direction on whether to
progress an Under 18 scheme, an Under 22 scheme, or a phased/pilot
approach, taking account of the scale of ongoing revenue costs,
delivery and capacity risks at peak times, and the absence of an
identified sustainable funding source for the more extensive Under
22 option.
 
Committee
direction will enable officers to focus further work on the
preferred approach, including detailed network analysis, operator
engagement and development of a funding strategy.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do nothing
The council avoids the direct financial commitment that a scheme
of this nature requires, and officer time and resource is then
available to be deployed on other projects. The potential benefits
of the scheme outlined in this report are not realised. 




 


 




11.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Implement a means tested
scheme
Learning from the Barnsley under 18s pilot indicates that
simple, universal schemes are more easily understood by families,
schools and operators, and achieve higher and more consistent take
up than targeted alternatives. By contrast, means testing
introduces significant administrative burden, requiring eligibility
checks, ongoing verification and data sharing arrangements that
increase cost, complexity and delivery risk, while potentially
delaying implementation. Such schemes also risk lower take up among
those most in need, as eligibility thresholds can exclude
households experiencing financial pressure but not meeting strict
criteria, and the application process itself can act as a barrier.
In addition, targeted offers can create stigma and confusion,
increasing the risk of inconsistent use and
enforcement.
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to approve recommendations for further development work on a potential free travel pilot for children and young people, subject to funding parameters and network analysis.

content:
14.1


The Director of Commissioning and
Commissioning Officer introduced the report which explained that
the Children, Families and Youth grant will bring together five
funding streams into a single consolidated grant and will be worth
£41.9 million to Sheffield over the three years of the
multi-year Settlement. It outlined the overview of the
grants and requested delegated authority
of:
 
·      
the FFPP funding and the Pupil Premium Plus Post-16 Grant to the
Strategic Director of Children’s
Services
·      
the HAF funding to the Director of Integrated
Commissioning.




 


 




14.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children
and Families Policy Committee:-
 

a)   
Note the developments and plans within the programme that are held
in the Children, Families and Youth grant. This includes the
Families First Partnership Programme, the Pupil Premium Plus
Post-16 activity and the Holiday Activities and Food
programme.

b)   
Approve the delegation of the Families First Partnership Programme
Funding and the Pupil Premium Plus Post-16 Grant to the Strategic
Director of Children’s Services.

c)   
Approve the delegation of the Holiday Activities and Food Grant to
the Director of Integrated Commissioning
including:
                                              
i.    
award new grants from any programme
underspend
                                             
ii.    
withdraw funding as necessary and in line with this report and the
conditions of the grant funding
agreements.

d)   
Approve the Holiday Activities and Food delivery approach and model
which has run successfully since 2021.

e)   
Approve the allocation of Holiday Activities and Food grant funding
to delivery partners including schools, VCFSE partners, and
organisations that will provide a vast range of cultural and
sporting activities across Sheffield.




 


 




14.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




14.3.1


FFPP
 
The ambition is
to build on existing good practice in the city to further improve
the network of services, processes and interactions that aim to
help children, young people, and families from the earliest
opportunity through to the highest level of need. If we continue to
develop our system, we will see vulnerable families thrive,
becoming empowered to become resilient over time and build
connections to their local community. Our local services will also
be joined-up, flexible and responsive to new challenges, becoming
sustainable for the long term creating stronger multi-agency
partnerships which work together to understand local trends,
predict emerging need, and respond to those needing additional
help. It is therefore essential that we continue our ambitions with
the full approval of the committee.




 


 




14.3.2


The Pupil Premium Plus Post-16
 
This element of the grant provides a flexible and responsive
funding stream that enables the Virtual School to strengthen
post?16 education, wellbeing and transition outcomes for
looked?after young people and care leavers. Continued approval is
essential to ensure Sheffield can sustain targeted, evidence?based
interventions aligned to statutory Virtual School duties, support
multi?agency practice, and respond quickly to individual needs
identified through the PEP process. The requirement to complete and
submit the annual Pupil Premium plus Post?16 Virtual School Head
Evaluation Survey to the Department for Education also creates an
important accountability mechanism, reinforcing the need for robust
oversight of expenditure, impact, and
delivery.




 


 




14.3.3


HAF
 
This decision will secure the continued delivery of the Holiday
Activities with Food (HAF) Programme, which provides essential
holiday activities and nutritious meals to some of the most
vulnerable children in Sheffield. The programme plays a vital role
in supporting the council’s wider ambitions to improve health
and wellbeing, reduce inequality, and ensure that all children have
access to positive opportunities during school
holidays.




 


 




14.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




14.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Deliver the HAF programme in house by
the Council:
 
While this would provide direct control over delivery, The
Council does not currently fund or deliver holiday or food
provision for children and young people. Establishing this capacity
would require significant investment in infrastructure and
staffing, and therefore would be unable to directly reach or
deliver holiday activities to eligible
cohorts




 


 




14.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Do not accept the DfE HAF
Grant:
 
Declining the grant would mean forfeiting funding to deliver
holiday activities and food for approximately 26,000 children in
our area who are eligible for free school meals. Without this
funding, the Council would be unable to provide high quality
holiday activities and food during the Easter, Summer, October and
Christmas school holidays. This would increase the risk of holiday
hunger and reduce access to enrichment opportunities for vulnerable
children, undermining statutory duties and local priorities around
child wellbeing and inclusion.




 


 




14.4.3


The preferred approach is to continue to deliver HAF through a
partnership model, building on five years of successful delivery
and strong relationships with schools, voluntary and community
sector organisations, and local providers. This approach maximises
reach, leverages existing expertise, and ensures activities are
accessible and culturally appropriate.
topline: The Education, Children and Families Policy Committee has decided to consolidate funding streams into a single grant worth £41.9 million for children, families, and youth programs in Sheffield.

12.1


The
Assistant Director of Children and Families introduced the report
which recommended introducing annual increases to Skill Level Fees
in line with the National Minimum Allowance for 2027/28 and
2028/29, capped at 4% per year, providing carers with greater
financial certainty.
 
The
report also proposed allocation of funding to relaunch the Foster
Carer Loan Scheme, using £50,000 in 2026/27 to fund small
property adaptations with a target to create at least four
additional fostering spaces.




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Agree policy change that foster carer skill level fees will
increase in line with National Minimum Allowance for the financial
years 2027/28 and 2028/29 up to a maximum of
4%.
b)   
Agree that policy will be reviewed at the end of this time period.
c)   
Agree funding of £50k diverted from placement budget and
allocated to Foster Carer Loan Scheme




 


 




12.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




12.3.1


The proposed changes to fostering payments and
the relaunch of the Foster Carer Loan Scheme are essential to
ensuring that Sheffield City Council can meet its statutory
sufficiency duty and provide the right homes for children and young
people in care. Current payment structures have not kept pace with
inflation or regional market rates, and evidence from carers shows
that financial support is the area most urgently requiring
improvement to support recruitment and retention. Without action,
the Council risks further erosion of in?house fostering capacity,
limiting placement choice and increasing reliance on costly
external residential provision.




 


 




12.3.2


Introducing a clear,
inflation?linked mechanism for reviewing Skill Level Fees over the
next two years provides carers with much?needed certainty and helps
stabilise a workforce that plays a critical role in delivering
safe, nurturing homes for children. This aligns directly with the
Placement Sufficiency Strategy (2023 2026), which sets out the
Council’s commitment to expanding family?based care options
as the most effective and sustainable way to meet children's
needs.




 


 




12.3.3


Re?establishing the Foster Carer
Loan Scheme will enable the creation of additional in?house
placements through small?scale property adaptations, helping to
reduce out?of?area placements and improve children’s ability
to remain connected with their families, schools, and
communities.




 


 




12.3.4


Overall, these recommendations are
necessary to strengthen Sheffield’s fostering offer, improve
placement stability and sufficiency, and deliver better outcomes
for children and young people while reducing long?term financial
pressures on the Council.




 


 




12.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


Do Nothing - continue make
payments in line with current policy.
 
·      
Foster cares feel undervalued by the Local Authority and
resign.
·      
Failure to change would mean that in real terms carers have not
received an enhancement in recognition of the skill and commitment
they offer children in care for 7 years at a time of significant
increase in the cost of living.
·      
Continued annual negotiation regarding fostering allowances leads
to confusion and dissatisfaction.
·      
Our current policy does not champion our strategic commitments to
education and belonging
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to increase Skill Level Fees for foster carers and relaunch the Foster Carer Loan Scheme to create additional fostering spaces.

content:
13.1


The
Service Manager introduced the report which set out Sheffield City
Council’s approach to supporting care leavers by enabling
young people in foster care to remain with their former foster
carers beyond the age of 18, where that is in their best interests
and all parties agree. The policy aimed to provide a more gradual
and supported transition to adulthood, mirroring the experiences of
young people who continue to live at home with their families after
turning 18.




 


 




13.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Agree to the Policy for Staying Put Providers, with implementation
from 1 April 2026.




 


 




13.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




13.3.1


The recommendation to amend the Staying Put
Policy is driven by the need to ensure that our approach remains
fit for purpose in supporting care leavers as they transition to
adulthood. Since the last policy update in 2019, both practice and
the needs of young people have evolved, particularly in response to
the challenges posed by the Covid-19 pandemic and feedback from
foster carers and stakeholders. The current policy does not fully
reflect the realities of practice, nor does it address the concerns
raised about financial arrangements, parity between local authority
and independent fostering agency carers, and the clarity required
for both carers and young people. Amending the policy will ensure
that it is aligned with statutory guidance, incorporates best
practice, and provides a clear, fair, and sustainable framework for
Staying Put arrangements.
 
Furthermore, updating the policy is essential to
deliver on the Council’s strategic priorities of promoting
stability, belonging, and successful futures for care leavers. The
revised policy will strengthen our ability to recruit and retain
high-quality carers, ensure financial arrangements are transparent
and equitable, and support the sufficiency of placements within
Sheffield. By clarifying roles, responsibilities, and funding
mechanisms, the amended policy will help maximise positive outcomes
for young people, reduce the risk of placement breakdowns, and
ensure that Sheffield City Council continues to meet its legal and
moral obligations to care-experienced young people as they move
towards independence.




 


 




13.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




13.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Not
taking any action
 
If no action is taken, the policy
will remain outdated, and unclear wording will continue to create
confusion. As a result, staying put providers who were formerly
Independent Fostering Agency carers would still receive higher
payments than our in-house foster carers. The 2019 policy also
lacks sufficient detail regarding the Staying Put process, which
has led to inconsistent interpretation and poor practice over time.
By updating the policy, we can ensure clarity and set clear
expectations for all involved—social workers, staying put
providers, and the staying put coordinator—by defining roles,
responsibilities, and processes.




 


 




13.4.2


Alternative Option 2:
Resubmitting the proposed 2024 policy
 
The 2024 policy introduced
significant financial changes and highlighted that the 2019 Staying
Put policy does not clearly distinguish between a young person in
care and an adult living at home. It noted that continuing to pay
skills payments at the full rate does not reflect the shift in the
young person’s status to adulthood, nor the evolving role of
the Staying Put Provider in supporting the young person’s
journey towards independence and home ownership. Resubmitting this
and implementing such substantial financial changes could cause
further concern among foster carers, as many feel that reducing
Staying Put allowances would discourage participation in these
arrangements. This, in turn, could lead to instability for young
people at a particularly vulnerable stage, forcing them to seek
alternative housing options. The proposed policy aims to clarify
financial arrangements for Staying Put carers and addresses
previously undefined sections. The only major financial impact
relates to Independent Fostering Agency carers, whose payments
would be aligned with those of Local Authority carers. This is
considered reasonable, and the payment is deemed sufficient to
support the young person.
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to approve a policy to support care leavers by allowing young people in foster care to stay with their former foster carers beyond the age of 18.

content:
8.1


The
Director of belonging introduced the report which informed the
Committee that the Group had been convened and outlined its
purpose, scope and intended reporting timescales. It was stated
that the Group would carry out its work during Spring 2026 and
would report its findings and recommendations to the June 2026
Committee meeting.




 


 




8.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Notes that a Task & Finish Group on promoting a smartphone-free
childhood has been convened and will hold its first meeting on 23
March 2026.
b)   
Endorses the proposed Terms of Reference and scope of the Group as
set out in Appendix A.
c)   
Agrees that the Task & Finish Group will report its findings,
conclusions and recommendations to the June 2026
Committee.




 


 




8.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




8.3.1


The decision is recommended in response to
concerns raised by local parents about the impact of early
smartphone and social media use on children’s wellbeing,
online safety and development. The establishment of a Task &
Finish Group provides a structured and transparent way for members
to examine the evidence, engage with partners and families, and
consider how the Council can best offer support within its role.
The Group will enable informed and proportionate recommendations to
be brought back to Committee for future decision
making




 


 




8.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




8.4.1


Do
nothing
 
The Committee could choose to take
no further action. This option was discounted because parents have
raised significant concerns about children’s wellbeing and
online safety, and doing nothing would not respond to the clear
level of community interest.




 


 




8.4.2


Refer the issue solely to the
Sheffield Safeguarding Children
Partnership
 
Officers considered managing the
issue entirely through existing safeguarding structures. While
safeguarding partners will be engaged, this option alone was
rejected as it would not give elected members a clear role in
shaping policy or responding to the wider educational and community
aspects identified
topline: The Director of belonging has decided to establish a Task & Finish Group on promoting a smartphone-free childhood in response to concerns raised by local parents about the impact of early smartphone and social media use on children's wellbeing, online safety, and development.

11.1


The Strategic Commissioning
Manager introduced the report which proposed continuing and
expanding the Medical Needs Education Service, currently provided
by Nexus Multi Academy Trust, for two years from September 2026.
The current 130 places would expand to
169.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children
and Families Policy Committee:-
 

a)   
Approves the commissioning of the Medical Needs Education Service
for two years from September 2026, with an estimated total cost of
£4.68m.

b)   
Notes that the expansion will increase capacity from 130 places to
161 places in Year 1 and to 169 places in Year 2, whilst keeping
the average cost per place below
£14,200.




 


 




11.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




11.3.1


A two year commission that continues and expands the
Medical Needs Education Service will allow the Council to meet its
statutory duties in regard to providing
education for children and young people with medical
needs.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Do nothing when the existing contract expires. This
option was rejected because it would leave the Council unable to
meet its statutory duties relating to pupils with medical needs

11.4.2


Providing the service in-house. This option was rejected
as the Council does not have the expertise or staffing required for
this delivery and could not mobilise this in time for the start of
the commission. As above, this would leave the Council unable to
meet its statutory duties.
topline: The Education, Children and Families Policy Committee has decided to approve the commissioning of the Medical Needs Education Service for two years, expanding capacity to 169 places.

content:
10.1


The
Assistant Director of Children and Families introduced the report
which sought approval to expand Sheffield’s children’s
residential care provision through the creation of a new two?bed
home designed specifically for children under the age of 12 who
require safe, stable, and nurturing accommodation within the city.
The proposal responded to rising demand, increasing placement
costs, and a shortage of suitable local homes, particularly for
younger children, while supporting the Council’s statutory
sufficiency duty and its Placement Sufficiency Strategy for
Children Looked After and Care Leavers
2023–2026.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That Education, Children and Families Policy
Committee:-
 
a)   
Approve the expansion of Sheffield’s children’s homes
provision through the establishment of two new two?bed residential
home for children under 12.
b)   
Approve the diversion of funding from the existing placement
revenue budget to meet the ongoing operational costs of the new
home.




 


 




10.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




10.3.1


Sheffield City Council, as a corporate parent,
has a statutory duty to ensure, as far as reasonably practicable,
that there is sufficient, appropriate accommodation within the
local area to meet the needs of looked?after children. Rising
demand, increasing placement costs, and a shortage of specialist
local provision for younger children mean that the current
sufficiency duty cannot be met without creating additional in?city
residential capacity. Establishing a new two?bed home specifically
for children under 12 will address a clear gap in provision and
support the delivery of the Placement Sufficiency Strategy for
Children Looked After and Care Leavers
2023–2026.




 


 




10.3.2


Expanding local children’s
homes will enable more young people to remain in Sheffield,
maintain family, school, and community connections, and benefit
from trauma?informed, developmentally appropriate care designed to
improve long?term outcomes. The proposal also supports longer?term
financial sustainability by reducing dependence on high?cost
external placements and increasing opportunities for children to
step down into foster care, contributing to both improved outcomes
and more efficient use of resources.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do
Nothing Rejected
 
Young people continue to live in
high cost out of city placements away from local connections. There
are insufficient placements in the market that meet the specific
needs of the cohort.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Local
Market Commissioning
 
Expansion of local in-house
children’s homes forms part of the portfolio’s wider
sufficiency. Engagement with private providers to ensure that the
right homes are developed for our children and young people
continues. This option is not ruled out and works alongside
development of in-house provision.
topline: The Sheffield City Council has decided to expand children's residential care provision by creating a new two-bed home for children under 12.

content:
To seek approval for the contract award to
Newton Consulting
Limited as the transformation programme delivery partner for
Adult Care and Wellbeing.





a)


Approval of a 2-year
and £9.1m contract award to Newton Consulting Limited as
delivery partner for the medium-term transformation programme for
Adult Care & Wellbeing.
 




b)


Noting the required
mobilisation of internal resources to support the transformation
programme as referred to this report.




 

The award of this contract will introduce and
develop key skills and best practice across Adult Care and
Wellbeing services.  This will enable
the service to align resource management with the strategic
priority to improve outcomes for the people of Sheffield.
 
The contract award will enable the Adult Care
and Wellbeing directorate to commission and deliver quality
services sustainably as part of a long-term financial strategy.
 
The selection of Newton Consulting Limited as
the transformation partner will accelerate the directorate’s
ability to meet financial targets, establishing a foundation for
manageable growth in the 2026/27 financial year.

Alternative Option 1: Do nothing
·      
The Council could choose not to implement a transformation
programme through a delivery partner and continue to deliver
savings and improvements on an annual cycle. While planned savings
have been delivered over the last five years, this has not been at
the pace required to be financially sustainable.
Alternative Option 2: Deliver internally
·      
Recruiting a specific workforce to design and implement the
transformation programme may cost less than the recommended
option.  However, the recruitment would
be labour and time intensive, and there is not the range of
specific skills and experience required within the Council to
deliver the programme successfully and at pace.  This option would also commit to longer-term
resources for change management, whereas the preferred approach is
to transfer to business as usual and self-management from year
2.
Alternative Option 3: Service by Service
improvement
·      
The Council could choose to enable individual service areas to
develop and implement specific changes associated with agreed aims
and ambition. This has been rejected because it would not achieve
the ‘one council’ approach and the holistic outcomes
and financial benefits envisaged in the Council Plan and the Future
Sheffield Programme.
topline: The Strategic Director, Adults' Care and Wellbeing has decided to approve a £9.1m contract award to Newton Consulting Limited for the transformation programme delivery partner for Adult Care and Wellbeing in Sheffield.

content:
The Bereavement & Coronial Service is
undertaking a comprehensive review of its service offer for
Sheffield’s Muslim community The review aims to ensure the
city’s bereavement and burial services meet the specific
religious and cultural requirements of residents of the Muslim
faith.

 




9.1


The Committee
considered a report of the Executive Director of Neighbourhood
Services which provided an update on progress on the city-wide
review of its burial and cremation provision, since the review
began in January 2026.  The report
sought Committee endorsement of the proposed approach for the next
phase of the review (including wider public consultation), and
confirmed the process for bringing back the final recommendations
for decision later in
2026




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy
Committee Policy Committee:-

(a) 
Notes the progress made to date on the review of Sheffield City
Council’s bereavement and burial service offer for Muslim
residents;

(b) 
Approves the proposed next phase of work, including continued
engagement, benchmarking and operational
analysis;

(c) 
Endorses the approach for developing final recommendations,
including stakeholder workshops, wider public consultation and
operational insight gathering;
and

(d) 
Requests a further report later in 2026 setting out the final
evidence-based recommendations and proposed implementation
plan.




 


 




 


 




9.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The proposed approach enables the Council to
respond appropriately to the concerns raised by residents and
community partners regarding whether the current burial offer fully
meets the religious and cultural requirements of the Muslim
community. Questions raised at Full Council, correspondence with
community representatives and recent engagement activity all
demonstrate a clear expectation that these matters should be
examined in a structured and meaningful way. Proceeding with the
review allows the Council to consider these issues thoroughly and
draw on a broad range of insight.




 


 




9.3.2


This decision will also support the development
of robust, evidence based recommendations that reflect both the
experiences of bereaved families and the operational realities of
delivering faith sensitive services. A comprehensive review will
help ensure that future planning is informed, sustainable and
aligned with the needs of Sheffield’s communities, while
strengthening partnership working and supporting the continued
delivery of inclusive, high quality bereavement
services.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do
Nothing
An alternative option would have been to take no
action and retain current arrangements without conducting any form
of review. This, however, was rejected due to the significant risks
outlined below.
 
Choosing to do nothing would have left existing
issues unaddressed, despite the concerns raised by residents and
community partners, through public forums and direct correspondence
with the Council, that more can be done to ensure burial service
provision meets the religious and cultural requirements of the
Muslim community. Furthermore, this issue has been brought to the
Council’s attention both at Communities, Parks and Leisure
Committee and Full Council, highlighting the need for proactive and
meaningful action to be taken.
 
In addition, choosing not to proceed with a
formal review would have risked undermining confidence in the
service at a time when both Elected Members and community partners
have anticipated that this work would be taken forward. Questions
raised publicly, alongside continued engagement with community
partners such as SMBPF, demonstrate that residents are looking to
the Council to respond constructively to the issues they have
raised. Failing to act would have risked giving the impression that
these concerns were not being taken seriously, while also limiting
the service’s ability to plan effectively for the future in
light of demographic change and increasing pressure on burial
provision.
 
Moreover, choosing to do nothing would fail to
acknowledge the feedback gathered from the 2024 consultation and
cross-party Task & Finish group, which recommended this
review.




 


 




9.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Taking an alternative,
expedited approach:
 
Another option would have been to take forward
the review using a different approach, drawing primarily on the
information already available through earlier consultation,
correspondence from residents and discussions with community
partners. While this may have allowed recommendations to be
developed more quickly, it was not recommended. Proceeding in this
way would have limited the opportunity to hear from a wider range
of voices across the Muslim community and would not have enabled
the deeper engagement required to fully understand the issues
raised and the lived experience of those
affected.
 
Moreover, this approach would have reduced the
scope for further benchmarking and operational analysis, which are
important in ensuring that future recommendations are thorough,
evidence based and sustainable. Given the significance of this
work, it is essential to ensure perspectives from across the Muslim
community are integrated fully, and that sufficient time is taken
to complete the review comprehensively. For these reasons, this
option was not considered suitable.
topline: The Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy Committee has decided to approve the next phase of a review to ensure burial services meet the religious and cultural requirements of Sheffield's Muslim community.

content:
Sheffield City Council to enter into a formal
grant agreement with Sheffield Hallam University and provide
operational management of two work programmes within the Sheffield
‘Place’ Investment, delivering against agreed outcomes
for the ‘Community Development’ and ‘Move
Well’ work areas. The investment period is two years (April
2026- March 2028). Investment into Sheffield City Council will
cover staff salaries (Sport, Leisure & Events team) plus allow
for investment into VCSE community organisations to deliver
community-based health and wellbeing services

 




11.1


The Committee
considered a report of the Executive Director of Neighbourhood
Services which provided an overview of the Sport England
‘Place’ Investment secured by Sheffield from April 2026
to March 2028.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Communities, Parks, and Leisure Policy
Committee  Policy
Committee:-

(a) 
Approves the Council becoming the accountable body for the grant
funding of £1,018,094.34 from Sheffield Hallam University
Services Limited, subject to the terms of the funding not being
materially different to those outlined in this
report.

(b) 
Approves the Council entering into a formal grant agreement with
Sheffield Hallam University Services Limited for grant funding of
£1,018,094.34, subject to the terms of the grant agreement
not being materially different to those outlined in this
report.




 


 




 


 




11.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




11.3.1


The recommendation to approve the Council
becoming accountable body for and entering into a formal grant
agreement for grant funding of £1,018,094.34 from Sheffield
Hallam University Services Limited ensures a continued strong
reputational position with national, regional, and local sport and
physical activity partners.




 


 




11.3.2


By accepting investment, SCC can invest in
community services across the five focus communities, ensuring
increased opportunities for residents to improve their health and
wellbeing, and ensuring capacity growth of the VCSE
sector.




 


 




11.3.3


The expansion of the Move Well, will ensure more
residents with long term health conditions can feel support and
motivated to improve their health, and benefit from more connected
and systematic healthcare pathways.




 


 




11.3.4


Whilst there is a small risk in entering into an
agreement and adhering to Sport England terms and conditions, it is
felt that benefits of delivering on this project, both to residents
and reputationally, significantly outweigh these
risks.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Do not accept the £1,018,094.34 investment
and do not enter into a grant agreement with Sheffield Hallam
University Services Limited.
 
Advantages

·      
The Council would avoid any financial, operational or delivery risk
associated with managing the grant and meeting Sport
England’s
compliance, monitoring, and reporting
requirements.

·      
No additional management or governance burden would fall to the
Council.
 
Disadvantages

·      
SCC was identified by NCSEM and partner organisations as the
preferred delivery body for the Community Development &
Services and Move Well work programmes due to its impartiality,
established governance arrangements, and proven experience in
delivering and overseeing high quality physical activity, health,
and wellbeing services. Declining this role would create a
reputational risk with national, regional, and local
partners.

·      
It is unlikely that an alternative organisation would be able to
assume delivery of these elements at short notice, creating a
significant risk that the funding could not be deployed as intended
and may need to be returned to Sport
England.

·      
Failure to accept the funding would result in missed opportunities
to invest in priority neighbourhoods, expand the Move Well service,
and strengthen community led delivery and VCSE capacity, limiting
the Council’s
ability to address physical inactivity and health
inequalities.

·      
Declining the investment would weaken
SCC’s
strategic position within the city’s physical activity and
health system and could reduce future opportunities to secure
external funding and influence programme
design.
topline: The Communities, Parks, and Leisure Policy Committee has decided to approve a grant agreement with Sheffield Hallam University for community development and health programs.

content:
The Library Collection Management Framework
sets out the principles and practices for the selection, purchase,
management, promotion and disposal of stock (also called
Collections) within Sheffield Libraries. The proposed Collection
Management Framework for Non-Lending Material outlines our approach
to managing the material currently stored in the basement of the
Central Library, which includes approximately six miles of
shelving. The proposal sets out an approach to evaluating the non
-lending material and subsequently defines a clear process for
retaining, rehoming, donating or selling items that do not meet the
retention criteria.





10.1


The
Committee considered a report of the Executive Director of
Neighbourhood Services which sought approval for a framework for
non-lending material in the library service, particularly in the
Central Library
Stack.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY:
That the Communities, Parks and
Leisure Committee Policy
Committee:-

(a) 
Approves the Collection Management Framework for
Non-Lending Material;
and

(b) 
Notes that a costed proposal to deliver this
framework will be developed to form part of Council business
planning for the 2027/28 financial
year.




 


 




 


 




10.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The Non-Lending Framework is
designed to complement the Library Collection Management Framework
for the Council’s lending stock. It will ensure a consistent
approach when managing library
material.




 


 




10.3.2


The Committee’s approval of
this framework and its subsequent implementation will make
non-lending material more accessible to the public through
digitisation, exhibitions and other promotions; to better reflect
Sheffield’s communities and reach new audiences and
customers.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Work on
Non-Lending Material without a
framework
This alternative has been rejected
because without a framework work on non-lending material will lack
structure and consistency. This risks making important material
less accessible and lacks transparency about how decisions will be
made.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Do no work
on Non-Lending Material
To care for our material and make
it more accessible we need to assess and curate it so that we can
prioritise material for promotion and digitisation. If we do no
work on non-lending material some of Sheffield’s cultural
treasures will remain inaccessible. This option also has risks
that:

·      
Material that might be more accessible with our
partners remains inaccessible in the
library

·      
Potential discovery of important items does not take
place

·      
Material cannot be valued
accurately

·      
The material risks degradation if not
assessed.

·      
The Library, Archive and Information Service holds
more material than it needs, incurring operational costs for
storage.
topline: The Communities, Parks and Leisure Policy Committee has decided to approve a Collection Management Framework for Non-Lending Material in Sheffield Libraries.

estimated value of £1.4m. This is subject to the number of
parking transactions / revenue over the 4-year period.

b)   
Approves that the operator transaction fee will
continue to be absorbed by the Council as part of the new cashless
parking contract.




 


 




10.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




10.3.1


The recommendation to
commission a new cashless parking contract through a competitive
procurement process is to make sure the Council secures the best
possible service and value for money. Running a competitive
exercise allows different providers to be assessed fairly, helping
to ensure the chosen system is reliable, easy to use, and able to
meet both current demand and future needs. It also supports
transparency, compliance with procurement rules, and the
opportunity to benefit from improved technology and innovation in
parking services.




 


 




10.3.2


Continuing to absorb the operator transaction
fee reflects the Councils commitment to keeping cashless parking
simple and accessible for everyone. By covering this cost, the
Council helps remove any additional financial burden on users,
which encourages uptake of digital payments and supports smoother
parking management overall. It also helps maintain a consistent
customer experience while reducing reliance on physical payment
infrastructure.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do nothing
 
If a new cashless parking contract was not
procured, residents, visitors and businesses would lose a
convenient way to pay for parking. People without easy access to
cash or Pay & Display machines would be particularly affected,
creating barriers for disabled users, older people, visitors and
those unfamiliar with the city.
 
Without a cashless option, it would be harder
for users to pay quickly and correctly. This would likely lead to
higher levels of accidental non-compliance, more appeals and
complaints, and increased pressure on parking enforcement and
customer services.
 
Sheffield currently has 266 active cashless
parking sites across the city. Within this network, 32 locations
operate exclusively as cashless parking zones, meaning that no
other payment options are available at these sites. The absence of
alternative payment methods at these locations highlights the
importance of maintaining a cashless parking contract. It
demonstrates that a 'do nothing' approach, where no new contract is
procured, is not viable. Without a cashless payment solution in
place, users would be unable to pay for parking at these sites,
resulting in significant inconvenience for residents, visitors and
businesses and undermining the effectiveness of the parking
system.




 


 




10.4.2


Alternative Option 2: National Parking
Platform
 
Discussions have been held with the National
Parking Platform (NPP) and consideration was given in entering a
contract with the provider. The NPP is a not-for-profit, open
platform that connects multiple parking service providers to
hundreds of locations nationwide. Instead of asking drivers to
download an app, it integrates the ones they already use,
supposedly making parking simple, seamless, and consistent
everywhere.
 
Created by the Department for Transport and
now run independently, the NPP is governed by Local Authorities,
service providers, and the British Parking Association.
 
Consideration was given to SCC joining the
National Parking Platform, reportedly used by councils such as
Liverpool, Coventry and Oxfordshire. This would have allowed a
direct award for the procurement due to how the platform was
established. There were both advantages and disadvantages to
joining the platform, which are outlined in the table below.
topline: The Environmental Services and Regulation Policy Committee has decided to approve a new cashless parking contract to modernize parking services and improve convenience for residents and visitors.

content:
The Intervention and Enforcement Policy
provides guidance for Council officers, landlords and members of
the public on the principles and processes which will apply when
enforcement action is considered or taken. It also provides a
background to the legislation and guidance on which the policy is
based. The Renters Rights Act will introduce new powers and duties
aimed at giving renters much greater security and stability and
will be the most significant shake-up of landlord and tenant law
for over 35 years.





11.1


The Committee
considered a report of the Director of Housing Services which
outlined updates to the Private Housing Standards Intervention and
Enforcement Policy and the Civil Penalties Policy following the
Renters’ Rights Act
2025




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Housing Policy
Committee:-

(a) 
Approves the contents of the amended Private Housing Standards
Intervention and Enforcement Policy, attached as Appendix 1 and
agrees that this policy shall be implemented and take effect from
the 1st May 2026;

(b) 
Approves the Civil Penalties Policy, attached as Appendix 2 and
agrees that this policy shall be implemented and take effect from
the 1st May 2026;

(c) 
Grants delegated authority to the Director of Housing Services, in
consultation with the Chair of the Housing Policy Committee, to
make where necessary any minor amendments and updates to the policy
required, in order to reflect any organisational or further
legislative changes which take place;
and

(d) 
Congratulates the Private Housing Standards team on taking the most
prosecutions in the past 10 years of any local authority under the
Protection From Eviction Act 1977, and enforcing housing standards,
thereby protecting tenants in the private rented
sector.




 


 




 


 




11.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




11.3.1


The recommendations are being made to ensure that
Sheffield City Council can meet its new statutory duties under the
Renters’ Rights Act 2025. The Act introduces the most
significant reforms to landlord and tenant law in over three
decades and places clear legal obligations on local authorities to
enforce the new tenancy rights, and protections for private
renters. In order for the Council to lawfully exercise these duties
from 1 May 2026, the existing Private Housing Standards
Intervention and Enforcement Policy and the Civil Penalties Policy
must be updated to reflect the expanded enforcement powers, new
offences, and increased financial penalty thresholds introduced by
the Act.




 


 




11.3.2


Updating these policies will also ensure that the
Council continues to provide a transparent, consistent, and robust
regulatory framework for the private rented sector. The changes
will support the delivery of safer, more secure housing for
residents, strengthen the Council’s ability to act against
unlawful practices, and ensure that enforcement decisions are
aligned with current legislation and national guidance. Without the
proposed amendments, the Council would be unable to implement the
Act effectively or take lawful enforcement action, which would
undermine tenant protections and expose the authority to legal and
operational risks.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Alternative Option
1:
To not approve the changes to these policies
would result in Sheffield not being able to implement the Act
lawfully, therefore not providing the increased protection to
tenants and likely being unable to take any enforcement action.
Therefore, there is no alternative option as these changes must be
made to ensure the service can regulate the private housing sector
lawfully.
topline: The Housing Policy Committee has decided to approve updated policies in response to the Renters' Rights Act 2025, impacting stakeholders in the private rented sector.

content:
12.1


The Committee
considered a report of the Executive Director of Neighbourhood
Services which proposed that the Council formally register with the
Energy Ombudsman, in line with new statutory requirements for all
heat suppliers.




 


 




12.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Housing Policy Committee:- approves the
Council’s registration with the Energy Ombudsman via deed
poll.




 


 




 


 




12.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




12.3.1


The council is required to register with the
Energy Ombudsman because new national legislation makes membership
of the Ombudsman’s dispute-resolution scheme a legal
obligation for all heat suppliers. This ensures that heat network
customers have access to an independent, impartial route for
escalating unresolved complaints, if we have been unable to resolve
the complaint through the standard SCC complaint process. covering
issues such as billing, service failures, and poor customer
experience. Registration aligns the council with wider reforms that
strengthen consumer protection and expand access to redress under
the updated energy regulatory framework. Although the registration
carries no direct procurement value, it represents a long-term
contractual commitment with annual fees and ongoing compliance
expectations and therefore requires formal committee approval. This
decision ensures legal compliance, supports fair treatment of
residents, and reinforces the council’s commitment to
transparent and accountable service
delivery.




 


 




 


 




12.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




12.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Do
nothing
This option was considered but discounted because
regulatory requirements mandate that we register with the Energy
Ombudsman.

Decision

The proposed LaNTP
and RSF programmes balances the availability of funding sources
with local and national policy to give a clear focus for the
2025/27 financial year, with an opportunity for changes to be
considered by Committee that could be made over the remainder of
the programme. The proposed programme is extensive and ambitious

internal and external funding sources and staff resources to

economic and societal needs.




 


 




 


 




10.4

10.4.1

not being delivered. Both the LaNTP and
the RSF programmes would not be introduced and the opportunity for
economic, environmental and societal benefits will be missed.




 


 




10.4.2


It would also be possible to consider a
different balance between types of schemes as part of the
programme. However, it is felt that the proposed programme achieves
a good balance of economic, environmental and societal benefits to
the communities and businesses in Sheffield.

11.1


The Committee considered a report of the
Executive Director, City Futures which outlined details of the
consultation response to proposals to introduce a 20mph speed limit
in Beaver hill and Arbourthorne, report
the receipt of objections to the Speed Limit Order and set out the
Council’s response.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the
Transport, Regeneration and Climate Policy Committee approves that
the Beaver Hill and Arbourthorne 20mph
Speed Limit Order be made, as advertised, in accordance with the
Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984.
 
Objectors will then be informed of the
decision by the Council’s Traffic Regulations team and the
order implemented on street subject to no road safety issues being
identified through a Road Safety Audit (RSA) at the detailed design
stage.




 


 




 


 




11.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




11.3.1


The adoption of the Sheffield 20mph Speed
Limit Strategy established the principle of introducing sign-only
20mph speed limits in all suitable residential areas. Reducing the
speed of traffic in residential areas should, in the long term,
reduce the number and severity of collisions, reduce the fear of
accidents, encourage sustainable modes of travel and contribute
towards the creation of a more pleasant, cohesive environment.




 


 




11.3.2


Having considered the response from the public
and other consultees it is recommended that the 20mph speed limit
in Beaver Hill be implemented as, on balance, the benefits of the
scheme in terms of safety and sustainability are considered to
outweigh the concerns raised.




 


 




11.3.3


It is also recommended that the 20mph speed
limit in Arbourthorne be implemented
for the same reasons as above.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives
Considered and Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Retention of existing
speed limit in the area (do nothing)
 
This would be contrary to the delivery of the
Sheffield 20mph speed limit strategy and would be detrimental to
the Council’s active travel ambition and vision of safer
streets in the city.




 


 




11.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Reduce scope of scheme
to just outside schools
 
This is contrary to the council’s 20mph
speed limit strategy that commits to installing 20mph speed limits
on all suitable residential roads and would relatively reduce the
benefits.
topline: The Transport, Regeneration and Climate Policy Committee has decided to approve a 20mph speed limit in Beaver Hill and Arbourthorne in Sheffield.

content:
11.1


The
Public Health Practitioner introduced the report which sought
approval from the Finance and Performance Policy Committee to award
a grant of £105,000 over three years to Voluntary Action
Sheffield (VAS) to deliver Phase 3 of the Sheffield Food
Cooperatives project, and to provide authority for the Council to
enter into a grant agreement with VAS.
 
The
Committee was also asked to delegate authority to the Director of
Public Health to finalise, approve and sign the grant agreement and
to take all other steps necessary to implement this
decision.




 


 




11.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Finance and
Performance Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Approve a grant of £105,000 over 3 years (£35,000 per
year) to Voluntary Action Sheffield to deliver Phase 3 of the
Sheffield Food Cooperatives project, including the Council entering
into the grant agreement.




 


 




11.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




11.3.1


Provision of grant funding and entering into a grant agreement
will support Voluntary Action Sheffield to deliver the food
cooperatives project for three years, to strengthen and expand the
network food cooperatives network across the city. This will
support people in the most deprived areas of the city, including
those at risk of experiencing food insecurity, with access to bulk
sourced food at a low price.
 
At
present, each food cooperative member pays between £2 and
£5 a week (£104 to £260 a year) to access food to
the value of £1,040. There are 10 food cooperatives in
Sheffield as of March 2026, each typically having 20 members. This
demonstrates the success of the food cooperatives in supporting
people to access quality food at a low price.




 


 




11.3.2


The
food cooperatives, as part of the food strategy programme, will
enable resources to be directed to work towards a local food system
that is fairer, greener and healthier and continues to positively
impact on different groups.




 


 




11.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




11.4.1


Alternative Option 1: Provide grant funding for Voluntary
Action Sheffield to deliver the food cooperatives project for one
year (rather than three years).
 
This
would restrict Voluntary Action Sheffield’s ability to take a
longer term approach to developing the
food cooperatives. It would also restrict their ability to offer
job security to the Food Cooperative Officer funded through this
grant.




 


 




11.4.2


Alternative Option 2: Provide no grant funding for
Voluntary Action Sheffield to deliver the food cooperatives
project.
 
This
would limit the expansion of food cooperatives across the city. As
a result, fewer Sheffield residents who could access low-cost,
quality, surplus food through the food cooperatives
model.
topline: The Finance and Performance Policy Committee has decided to approve a grant of £105,000 over 3 years to Voluntary Action Sheffield for the Sheffield Food Cooperatives project.

content:
10.1


The
Finance Manager introduced the report which provided the Committee
with details of changes to the Council’s Non-Domestic Rates
Discretionary Relief Policy and sought approval to implement
Government changes to allow for flexible backdating of reliefs
subject to the policy and the implementation of new reliefs
introduced following the National Revaluation of Rateable
Values.




 


 




10.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Finance and
Performance Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Note the changes to the Non - Domestic Rates Discretionary Relief
Policy, including the ending, and amendment of exiting
reliefs.
b)   
Approve the change to backdating of Reliefs covered in this
policy.
c)   
Approve the implementation of Reliefs introduced as a result of the
National Revaluation of Rateable Values.




 


 




10.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




10.3.1


At a
time when businesses across the City are facing significant
challenges, increase in rateable values only add concern and
uncertainty. Given the power the Council has to award these reliefs
and provide financial support to businesses, and the responsibility
the Council has to protect its citizens, businesses, its own
finances and the services it provides wherever possible. It is
imperative that the Council implements these reliefs. In adopting
these fully funded Government reliefs, the Council is going a
significant way to meeting its obligations.




 


 




10.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




10.4.1


It is
an option for the Council not to exercise its discretion under
section 47 LGFA and not provide these reliefs for the periods set
by Government. However, as the aim of the reliefs is to provide
extra financial support (in addition to any statutory support and
other reliefs available to businesses) to certain categories of
businesses within the City that have been identified by Government
as being those most impacted by the National Revaluation of
Rateable Values. to not provide the support offered by these
reliefs would severely impact the ability of these businesses to
deal with the impact of significant increases in rate bills from
2026 onwards.




 


 




10.4.2


Further, given that the Council has a commitment to developing a
creative and prosperous City full of culture, learning, and
innovation develop a strong local economy, including a thriving
City Centre and Successful Centres across the City, and to support
sustainable local employment, it is not considered to be in the
best interests of the Council, businesses or rate payers to not
adopt the relief schemes as outlined in this report




 


 




10.4.3


Widening the scope of the policy
 
Under
the Council’s discretionary powers under Section 47 of the
LGFA it could also choose to widen the scope of the Policy in order
to;
 

·      
to include businesses that under the relevant Government guidance
are not intended to be eligible for relief.

·      
to increase the level of relief above the levels set out in the
Government guidance, e.g., increase Pub and Live Music Venue Relief
by more than 15%.
 
However, if the Council were to do any of the above, any awards
of relief to those additional businesses or awards made at higher
amounts, would not be funded by the Government and would have to be
funded in full by the Council.
 
Therefore, given the ongoing financial challenges faced by the
Council, it is not proposed that the Council uses its powers to
expand the scope of these relief schemes.
topline: The Finance and Performance Policy Committee has decided to approve changes to the Council's Non-Domestic Rates Discretionary Relief Policy to provide financial support to businesses facing challenges.

content:
9.1


The Assistant Director or Performance &
Insight introduced the report which presented the third quarterly
Outcomes Framework report to committee for the 2025/26 financial
year. It included current, historic and comparator data for the
Council Plan Outcome measures. In addition to measure data, the
report included more detailed narratives provided by measure owners
on strengths and challenges.




 


 




9.2


RESOLVED UNANIMOUSLY: That the Finance and
Performance Policy Committee:-
 
a)   
Note the Council Plan Outcomes Framework Q3 Report that evidences
our improvements and show distance travelled against each Council
Plan priority.
b)   
Agree to continue to receive quarterly reports that provide an
overview of performance against the Outcome measures, describing
performance strengths, challenges, interventions taken, and the
results of changes made.
c)   
Agree to include the proposed additional Outcomes Framework
measures through 2025/26.




 


 




9.3


Reasons for Decision




 


 




9.3.1


The
Outcomes Framework underpins how we measure progress and monitor
impact of the Council Plan. It is aligned to our four-year Medium
Term Financial Strategy and the outcomes
will increasingly become the focus for our budget, Directorate and
Service Plans.




 


 




9.3.2


Council
Plan Outcomes Framework performance provides measurable evidence of
distance travelled against the Council Plan as part of a systematic
process of robust corporate performance reporting.




 


 




9.3.3


To
ensure that Finance & Performance Policy Committee contributes
to the performance management process and drives improvement across
the organisation.




 


 




9.4


Alternatives Considered and Rejected




 


 




9.4.1


Previous decisions made require
officers to proceed with implementing the full performance
framework to underpin how we measure progress and monitor impact of
the Council Plan. It is aligned to our four-year Medium Term
Financial Strategy and the outcomes will
increasingly become enabling elements for our priority-based
budget, Directorate and Service plans going forwards and set a key
deliverable for the Council.




 


 




9.4.2


Beyond
some nuance of how we implement some details of the framework, the
measures, performance system and reporting cycles are agreed,
removing the alternative options available for implementation of
the framework.

content:
To commence re?tendering of the British Gas
Voidcare contract and to undertake soft
market testing, supported by the obtaining of a Waiver of Contract
Standing Orders until 30 June 2026.
The waiver is required to maintaincontinuity
of utility services for void properties while the Council resolves
outstanding financial and operational matters and progresses a
compliant procurement exercise.
 

The Director of Housing and Repairs:

Approves the decision to re?procure
a contract for the provision of utility supply and associated
management services for Housing void properties, replacing the
current arrangements associated with the British Gas Voidcare portal.
Approves the proposed procurement
strategy to undertake a compliant procurement exercise in
accordance with the Council’s Contract Standing Orders and
the Procurement Act 2023, for a contract term of up to four years
(initial term plus permitted extensions), within approved budget
provision.
Approves the delegation of authority
to the appropriate Director, in consultation with Commercial
Services and Legal Services, to:

Finalise the procurement
documentation,
Undertake soft market testing and
conduct the procurement exercise, and
Award the resulting contract to the
successful bidder in accordance with the approved strategy and
delegated authority.


Notes that a Waiver of Contract
Standing Orders is in place until 30 June 2026 to ensure continuity
of service while the procurement exercise is completed.

 

The decision is required for
legal, financial, and governance compliance in the management of
utilities for Housing void properties.
Re?procurement is necessary to
meet statutory obligations under the Procurement Act 2023 and
Contract Standing Orders.

Alternative Option 1
- Continue current arrangements / do nothing: Rejected.
Continues non?compliance, financial risk, and
audit exposure, with contractual ambiguity and uncertainty.
 
Alternative Option 2 - Extend/renew with
British Gas without competition: Rejected. Would
perpetuate procurement non?compliance and expose the Council to
challenge and reputational risk.
 
Alternative Option 3 - Immediate service
cessation: Rejected. Would jeopardise safety/continuity
for void properties and risks higher costs and operational
disruption. (Service need is ongoing.)

purpose:
To provide an update to the Committee on the
latest position regarding Endcliffe Lodge following the marketing

content:
To provide an update to the Committee on the
latest position regarding Endcliffe Lodge following the marketing
exercise that was carried out.





8.1


The Committee
considered a report of the Executive Director of Neighbourhood
Services, which asked it consider whether entering into lease
negotiations with the recommended operator was in the best interest
of the Endcliffe Park Charity and if so, to approve the
recommendation to authorise the Chief Property Officer in
consultation with the Director of Legal and Governance, to
negotiate the terms of the lease with the proposed lessee, and the
Director of Legal and Governance to prepare and complete all the
necessary legal documentation in accordance with the agreed terms
and in respect of a charge over title, following completion of the
previously approved marketing
process.




 


 




8.2


RESOLVED
UNANIMOUSLY: That the Charity Trustees
Sub-Committee:-
 

(a) 
Notes the contents of?the
report;
(b) 
Agrees that entering into lease negotiations with the recommended
operator is in the best interest of the?Endcliffe?Park
Charity;
(c) 
Approves an exclusivity period of 6 months, with the ability to
extend by a further 6 if needed subject to satisfactory progress to
that point, to allow for officers to negotiate and finalise the
detailed terms of the lease, on the basis of those terms set out in
the closed Appendices; and
(d) 
Delegates authority to the Head of Property Services in
consultation with the Head of Legal Services, the Chair, Deputy
Chair, and Group Spokesperson of this sub-committee, to approve
final terms and enter into legal
documentation.




 


 




 


 




8.3


Reasons for
Decision




 


 




8.3.1


The provision of further visitor facilities
alongside significant investment for the park, contributes to the
objects of the charity; ‘the provision and maintenance of a
park for “walks and pleasure
grounds.’




 


 




8.3.2


Bringing investment and an annual income allows
the Council as sole trustee to support the management and
maintenance of the park and in turn contribute to the charity
objects.




 


 




8.3.3


In addition:

·      
A valued Charitable historic building is brought back into active
use, preserving an important asset within the charitable
park.

·      
Much?needed investment is secured for Endcliffe Park Lodge,
reducing the risk of further deterioration and ensuring its
long?term sustainability.

·      
Enhanced recreation and leisure facilities are provided for
visitors, improving the overall experience within Endcliffe
Park.

·      
Reduced financial and maintenance liabilities for the Charity, as
responsibility for repairs and upkeep transfers to the
tenant.




 


 




8.4


Alternatives Considered and
Rejected




 


 




8.4.1


Alternative Option 1 – Do
nothing:
An alternative option would be not to proceed
with lease negotiations with the recommended operator. However,
this would mean no investment would be secured for Endcliffe Park
Lodge, resulting in no improvement to the facility and a loss of
potential rental income for the Charity, which directly supports
the ongoing management and maintenance of the park. This would
negatively affect the quality of the visitor experience and fail to
maximise the Charity’s assets. For these reasons, this option
has been rejected.




 


 




.4.2


Alternative Option 2 – Re-market the
opportunity:
We are satisfied that the marketing undertaking
identified the operator interest in this property and that
re-offering the site would not be a worthwhile process for the
Charity.
topline: The Charity Trustees Sub-Committee has decided to approve lease negotiations with a recommended operator for Endcliffe Lodge, aiming to bring investment and enhance visitor facilities in Endcliffe Park.

“walks and pleasure
grounds.’




 


 




9.3.2


Bringing investment and an annual income allows
the Council as sole trustee to support the management and
maintenance of the park and in turn contribute to the charity
objects.




 


 




9.3.3


In addition:

·      
If much?needed investment is secured for Norfolk Park, this will
reduce the risk of further deterioration and ensuring its long?term
sustainability.

·      
Enhanced recreation and leisure facilities are provided for
visitors, improving the overall experience within Norfolk
Park.

·      
Reduced financial and maintenance liabilities for the Charity, as
all maintenance and upkeep obligations rest ultimately with the
Charity.

Alternatives Considered and
Rejected

degrade. This would result in the park becoming a less desirable

recreational value. Infrastructure failure could result which would
have health and safety implications for park users. There would
also be implications and impact on the site’s heritage
status. These outcomes would not be in the interest of the
charity.
